anxiety-signs-and-treatment.name: Anxiety: signs, treatment and getting help
anxiety-signs-and-treatment.summary: Anxiety becomes a health problem when worry is hard to control and affects daily life. Talking therapy comes first, medicine is next, and help is available without a GP referral.
keyPoints: Some anxiety is a normal part of life; it becomes a concern when worry is hard to control and gets in the way of daily life.
Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, before medicine.
People in England can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is anxiety, and when does it become a problem?
body.body: Feeling anxious now and then is a normal part of life. Generalised anxiety disorder, or GAD, is a long-term condition in which a person feels anxious most days, about a wide range of situations rather than one event. That worry gets in the way of daily life.

body.heading: What are the signs?
body.body: Alongside worry, symptoms can include feeling restless, trouble concentrating or sleeping, tiredness, irritability, muscle tension, dizziness and heart palpitations (a pounding or fluttering heartbeat). Because many of these also occur in other conditions, a GP can help work out what is going on.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: The exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and several factors probably combine. Factors named in the sources include inherited genes, past stressful or traumatic experiences, a long-term painful health condition, and past drug or alcohol misuse.

body.heading: What happens at the GP appointment?
body.body: NICE advises a comprehensive assessment that looks at the number, severity and duration of symptoms, and also at the degree of distress and the effect on daily functioning. Where another condition such as depression is also present, NICE says the more severe disorder is generally treated first. A short two-question screen about feelings of anxiety and the ability to control worry may be used.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body: Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment before medication. Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is a talking therapy that looks at how thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another. CBT and applied relaxation are both talking therapies available on the NHS for GAD. NICE describes CBT-based self-help as a low-intensity step, with written or electronic materials worked through systematically over several weeks. If talking therapy is not enough, medicine is the next option, and the usual first choice is an SSRI, a type of antidepressant. NICE sets out treatment in steps, offering the least intrusive, most effective option first. Step 4 is for complex, treatment-resistant anxiety with marked impairment or a high risk of self-harm, and involves specialist care.

body.heading: What can people do themselves?
body.body: NHS self-help ideas include regular exercise, cutting back on caffeine, which may help reduce anxiety, and eating a healthy diet. The NHS suggests drinking alcohol in moderation and stopping smoking as part of looking after physical health. Many books and courses can teach ways of coping with anxiety.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says to speak to a GP if anxiety is hard to cope with and self-help is not enough. A GP can talk through treatment and refer on, and people can also refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service. Charities such as Mind, Rethink Mental Illness and Anxiety UK also offer support.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Anxiety is common and treatable, and there are several routes to help. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which local NHS trusts describe as free and available at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

depression-signs-and-getting-help.name: Depression: signs and getting help
depression-signs-and-getting-help.summary: Depression is more than feeling unhappy for a few days. The NHS describes lasting low mood and loss of interest, and treatment can include self-help, talking therapy and medicine.
keyPoints: Depression is more than feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days, and it can come with physical symptoms.
Treatment depends on severity and usually combines self-help, talking therapies and sometimes medicine.
People can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service, or a GP can refer them.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is depression?
body.body: The NHS describes depression as more than simply feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days. It can involve feeling sad for weeks or months, to the point that it interferes with work, social life and family life.

body.heading: What are the signs?
body.body: Some people also notice physical symptoms, such as tiredness, sleeping badly, changes in appetite or unexplained aches. The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms of depression last most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks. Low mood can improve after a short time, but feelings that last most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks may be a sign of depression. Many people with depression also have symptoms of anxiety. Aches and pains can also be part of the picture. Depression can range from mild to severe.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: Life-changing events such as bereavement, losing a job or giving birth can bring depression on. People with a family history of depression are more likely to experience it, and depression can also arise for no obvious reason.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: Treatment usually depends on how severe the depression is. It usually involves a combination of self-help, talking therapies and medicine. For mild depression, a GP can refer someone for talking therapies, or the person can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service. For moderate to severe depression, a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants is often recommended. People with severe depression may be referred to a specialist mental health team. For mild depression, a doctor may suggest watchful waiting, which means monitoring progress to see whether it improves, alongside lifestyle measures and guided self-help. The NHS describes exercise as one of the main treatments for mild depression, and guided self-help is usually based on the principles of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).

body.heading: How do antidepressants fit in?
body.body: Antidepressants are one of the treatment options, and SSRIs are usually the type prescribed first. Antidepressants do not work straight away; the NHS says it usually takes around a week before effects start to be noticed. The NHS advises that antidepressants are reduced gradually when they are stopped, to help avoid withdrawal symptoms, and that this should be done with the GP. The NHS says to contact a GP straight away if feelings of hopelessness or suicidal thoughts start, or get worse, after starting an antidepressant.

body.heading: When should someone get help?
body.body: A GP appointment is the usual first step for someone who thinks they may have depression. NHS talking therapies accept self-referral, so a GP is not the only way in.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life are present, the NHS advises asking for an emergency GP appointment, calling NHS 111, or calling Samaritans on 116 123 at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. In England, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2) for urgent help that is not an emergency, which trusts describe as available 24 hours a day. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

panic-attacks-what-they-are.name: Panic attacks: what they are and what helps
panic-attacks-what-they-are.summary: A panic attack is a rush of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat. The NHS describes how attacks pass and how talking therapy and medicine can treat repeated attacks.
keyPoints: A panic attack causes physical symptoms such as a pounding heart, fast breathing and shaking, and many people fear the next attack.
The NHS says a panic attack usually lasts between 5 and 20 minutes, although some last longer.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is offered for repeated panic attacks, and in England people can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is a panic attack?
body.body: A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear or anxiety. A single panic attack does not necessarily mean someone has panic disorder, which is when attacks keep coming back.

body.heading: What does it feel like?
body.body: Common physical signs include a pounding heart, fast breathing and shaking. The NHS says a panic attack usually lasts between 5 and 20 minutes. Panic can feel like heart or breathing problems, so the NHS advises speaking to a GP rather than self-diagnosing. The NHS says that although panic attacks are frightening, an attack will not cause physical harm.

body.heading: What can help during an attack?
body.body: The NHS advice is to stay where you are if you can, breathe slowly and deeply, and remind yourself that the attack will pass and is not life threatening. NHS self-help guides describe the feelings as normal bodily reactions that are not harmful, and suggest waiting for them to pass rather than adding frightening thoughts. Grounding techniques, such as focusing on the senses, can also help.

body.heading: How are repeated attacks treated?
body.body: Cognitive behavioural therapy is a recommended psychological treatment, and in England people can refer themselves to a talking therapies service or ask a GP to refer them. Medicines used include SSRI antidepressants, and a tricyclic antidepressant may be used if SSRIs are not suitable. NICE says psychological therapy, medicine and self-help have all been shown to work, and that the benefits of psychological treatment lasted longest.

body.heading: What causes panic disorder, and when should someone see a GP?
body.body: The exact cause of panic disorder is not fully understood, and it is thought to be probably a combination of physical and psychological factors. A GP asks the person to describe their symptoms and may carry out a physical examination to rule out other causes. The NHS says to see a GP if attacks keep happening.

body.heading: What can people do day to day?
body.body: The NHS suggests activities such as yoga and Pilates, breathing exercises for stress, and regular exercise to help ease anxiety. NHS self-help guides note that escaping or avoiding panic can stop an attack in the moment but can also keep the problem going.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Panic attacks are frightening but pass. If a person feels unable to stay safe, urgent help is open at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

nhs-talking-therapies-how-they-work.name: NHS talking therapies and how to self-refer
nhs-talking-therapies-how-they-work.summary: NHS talking therapies offer CBT and counselling for anxiety and depression. In England you can refer yourself, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
keyPoints: NHS talking therapies are free psychological treatments for anxiety and depression, such as CBT and counselling.
In England people aged 18 or over can usually refer themselves, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
In immediate danger, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS 111 has a mental health option for urgent help, and Samaritans (116 123) is free to call.

body.heading: What are NHS talking therapies, and what help do they offer?
body.body: NHS talking therapies services treat common problems such as anxiety and depression with psychological treatments. Treatments include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and counselling. Formats include a self-help workbook with a therapist's support, an online course, one-to-one sessions in person, by phone or by video, and group sessions. CBT is based on the idea that thoughts, feelings, behaviour and physical sensations are connected, and it helps people notice and challenge unhelpful patterns. It is an active, practical therapy that includes exercises and homework. Talking therapies can also help with mental health problems that come with long-term physical conditions, such as diabetes, heart conditions or long-term pain.

body.heading: Who can refer themselves?
body.body: People can refer themselves directly, without a referral from a GP. Eligibility is mainly about age and location: people aged 18 or over who live in England can self-refer, and some areas also accept 16 and 17 year olds. A diagnosed mental health condition is not needed. Some local services ask people to be registered with a GP in their area, so the local service's own page has the details. This route describes NHS talking therapies in England.

body.heading: What happens after referral?
body.body: Someone from the service usually gets in touch to carry out an assessment. The therapist then recommends a treatment based on the symptoms and how severe they are. Waiting times vary by area, so the local service can say how long the wait is.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Talking therapies are not an emergency service. For urgent help, the routes below are open at any time. If someone is in immediate danger, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which NHS trusts describe as available at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.name: Supporting someone with a mental health problem
supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.summary: Listening, asking open questions and offering practical help are the NHS's main suggestions for supporting someone with a mental health problem, without forcing them to talk.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests telling the person you are worried, carrying on as usual, and offering to listen.
Open questions that start with how, what, where or when give the person room to answer in their own words.
The NHS advises against forcing someone to talk or to get help.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: How can you start the conversation and help?
body.body: The NHS suggests telling the person that you are worried about them. It also suggests carrying on as usual, so the person is not treated differently because of what they are going through. Open questions that start with how, what, where or when are recommended. The NHS says not to force someone to talk to you. The NHS gives going with the person to professional appointments as an example of practical help.

body.heading: How can you point someone towards professional help?
body.body: For people who need more support, the NHS lists contacting a GP, calling NHS 111, or self-referring to NHS talking therapies. The NHS directs anyone who cannot cope or keep themselves safe to urgent support.

body.heading: What if the person wants to start talking?
body.body: The NHS guidance for people talking about their own mental health suggests choosing someone they trust who can offer the kind of support they need, and planning what to say. It notes that some people find it easier to talk while walking, travelling in a car or cooking, and that a person does not have to say everything at once. If the person chosen does not feel able to help, the NHS says not to take it personally.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If someone is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

loneliness-and-health.name: Loneliness and health: effects and what helps
loneliness-and-health.summary: Severe or long-lasting loneliness can affect mental and physical health, according to the NHS. Staying in touch, joining groups and asking a GP about social prescribing can help.
keyPoints: The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia, and of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression.
Regular contact with friends and family, joining a group or club, and volunteering are NHS suggestions for easing loneliness.
A GP can talk about social prescribing, which links people with a link worker for local support.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is loneliness, and is it a health issue?
body.body: Loneliness is the distress of feeling alone or disconnected, and it is not the same as spending time by yourself. The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia. It also says it might increase the risk of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression. Common triggers include bereavement, a break-up, moving away, becoming a parent or carer, and long-term illness.

body.heading: What helps with loneliness?
body.body: NHS suggestions include keeping in touch with friends and family. The NHS also suggests joining a group, for example around something you enjoy. Volunteering is another NHS suggestion. The NHS also suggests doing activities you enjoy. The NHS also suggests talking openly about how loneliness feels, and notes that comparing yourself with others, especially on social media, can make you feel lonelier. For older people, the NHS suggests keeping in touch by phone or video chat, and volunteering.

body.heading: What can a GP or the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS suggests speaking to a GP about social prescribing, which connects people with a link worker who can point to local support. NHS talking therapies can help with common problems such as stress, anxiety and depression. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with loneliness, because they can contribute to poor mental health. The NHS says a GP can help if low mood lasts or if things tried at home are not helping.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If loneliness feels overwhelming, free support lines are open at any time of day or night. If someone is in immediate danger, the NHS advice is to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), open at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.name: Grief and bereavement: what to expect
grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.summary: Grief is a natural response to loss, and the NHS says feelings usually ease gradually. A GP or bereavement service can help when grief is very strong or does not ease.
keyPoints: Grief is a normal response to loss, and the NHS says feelings of sadness should ease gradually over time.
NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief.
The NHS says to see a GP if someone is struggling to cope, or their own efforts are not helping.
In an emergency, with immediate danger to life, the NHS says to use 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 are routes to urgent support.

body.heading: What does grief feel like?
body.body: Grief can bring shock, numbness, sadness, exhaustion and anger. NHS inform says there is no deadline on feeling better or recovering after a bereavement. NHS inform describes delayed grief, when grief is not fully felt at the time, and says it is never too late to grieve. The NHS lists shock, sadness, tiredness, anger and guilt among common reactions to loss.

body.heading: What can help?
body.body: The NHS suggests talking to someone trusted, joining peer support, taking regular exercise and eating regular meals. The NHS advises against relying on alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with grief. Bereavement support organisations such as Cruse can help, and talking to others can bring comfort.

body.heading: When is it worth getting help?
body.body: The NHS says sadness should ease gradually with time, but medical help may be needed if someone feels increasingly depressed or anxious. It advises seeing a GP when someone is struggling to cope, has had low mood for more than two weeks, or finds their own efforts are not helping. People in England can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.

body.heading: Where can bereaved people and children find support?
body.body: The NHS has a page on grief after bereavement or loss and a separate page on children and bereavement. Cruse Bereavement Support offers a helpline and information on dealing with grief, and Child Bereavement UK and Winston's Wish support bereaved children and families.

body.heading: What is prolonged grief?
body.body: For some people, painful feelings do not ease as months go by, and the NHS says this may be prolonged grief disorder, which may need a clinician's assessment. Signs the NHS lists include difficulty accepting the death and suicidal thoughts, and it says to seek help from a GP, or urgent help if there are suicidal thoughts.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If grief brings thoughts of suicide, urgent help is available; NHS inform in Scotland points to NHS 111 for people in distress or despair. In an emergency, when someone is in immediate danger or has been physically harmed, the NHS says to use 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

menopause-symptoms-and-help-available.name: Menopause: symptoms and the help available
menopause-symptoms-and-help-available.summary: HRT is the main medicine for menopause symptoms, and non-hormone options exist. The NHS says a GP can talk through the options, and NICE advises discussing benefits and risks of HRT.
keyPoints: The NHS calls hormone replacement therapy (HRT) the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms.
NICE advises offering HRT for hot flushes and night sweats after discussing the short- and long-term benefits and risks.
Options that do not use hormones include cognitive behavioural therapy and lubricants or moisturisers for vaginal dryness.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of menopause?
body.body: NICE guidance covers hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal and urinary symptoms, and effects on mood. The perimenopause is the time of change before periods stop, and symptoms can begin then. The NHS lists hot flushes, night sweats, low mood or anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, difficulty sleeping and changes to periods. Others include headaches and migraines, joint and muscle pain, weight gain, skin changes and a lower sex drive. The NHS says a person may have a number of symptoms, or none. Menopause is confirmed once a person has had no period for 12 months. The NHS says menopause usually affects people between the ages of 45 and 55, though it can happen earlier.

body.heading: What is HRT?
body.body: The NHS says the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms is hormone replacement therapy, or HRT. Oestrogen comes as skin patches, a gel or spray, implants or tablets. Anyone who still has a womb also needs a progestogen to protect the womb lining.

body.heading: How soon does treatment work?
body.body: According to the NHS, hot flushes or night sweats often improve within a few weeks. Other symptoms, such as mood changes and vaginal dryness, can take a few months to improve.

body.heading: What are the benefits and risks?
body.body: The NHS says HRT can lower the risk of osteoporosis, the thinning of the bones. Some types of HRT slightly raise the risk of breast cancer, and HRT tablets carry a small increase in the risk of blood clots. Because benefits and risks differ from person to person, the NHS and NICE both describe a discussion with a clinician.

body.heading: What else is available?
body.body: Vaginal oestrogen, as a pessary, cream, gel or ring, can treat vaginal dryness and other genitourinary symptoms of the menopause. For people who cannot or choose not to take HRT, the NHS lists cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which can help with low mood and anxiety caused by menopause and perimenopause. Vaginal lubricants and moisturisers are also used. The NHS suggests that regular exercise may reduce hot flushes, and that spicy food, caffeine, smoking and alcohol can be triggers.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says people with menopause or perimenopause symptoms can talk to a GP about their options. The NHS advises seeing a GP about any vaginal bleeding after periods have stopped for 12 months or more, even if it has only happened once.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Menopause can affect mood and sleep. If low mood becomes severe or there are thoughts of self-harm, help is available at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

antenatal-care-on-the-nhs.name: NHS antenatal care: appointments and scans
antenatal-care-on-the-nhs.summary: The NHS offers antenatal appointments with a midwife, two ultrasound scans and optional screening tests. First pregnancies get at least 10 appointments, later ones around 7.
keyPoints: People having their first baby are offered at least 10 antenatal appointments and 2 ultrasound scans, and those who have had a baby before typically have around 7 appointments.
The booking appointment with a midwife is usually the first, and NICE recommends offering it by about 10 weeks of pregnancy.
Screening tests are optional, and NICE says a woman can accept or decline any part of any screening programme.
Exact schedules vary between local maternity services.

body.heading: What antenatal care does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says first-time mothers are offered at least 10 appointments and 2 ultrasound scans. People who have had a baby before typically have around 7 appointments. The exact schedule varies between local maternity services.

body.heading: What happens at the booking appointment?
body.body: The booking appointment is usually the first appointment with a midwife and can take around an hour. The NHS says the booking appointment should ideally happen before about 10 weeks of pregnancy, and NICE recommends offering it by 10 weeks. At this appointment, NICE recommends that staff discuss and offer screening for infectious diseases (HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B), sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, and fetal anomalies.

body.heading: What checks happen at later appointments?
body.body: Later appointments happen at intervals through pregnancy, and the midwife checks blood pressure, urine, bump size and the baby's movements.

body.heading: What scans are offered?
body.body: The scan offered at around 11 to 14 weeks, sometimes called the dating scan, shows how far along the pregnancy is and checks the baby's development. The 18 to 21 week scan, often called the anomaly or 20-week scan, looks at the baby's development and screens for 11 physical conditions.

body.heading: Are screening tests compulsory?
body.body: Screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes is offered in early pregnancy, and it is the woman's choice whether to have it. NICE says the woman can accept or decline any part of any of the screening programmes offered.

body.heading: What else does antenatal care cover?
body.body: The free flu vaccine is offered in every pregnancy, as is the whooping cough vaccine. Maternity services also give advice on supplements such as folic acid and vitamin D, and the NHS page sets out the amounts. Local maternity services vary in the exact schedule and in what they include, so the local service's own plan is the reference.

fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.name: Fever and rashes in children: when to get help
fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.summary: Most fevers in children can be looked after at home. The NHS says call 999 for signs such as a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade, and NHS 111 or a GP for a baby under 3 months.
keyPoints: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home, with plenty of fluids and regular checks, including overnight.
Call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, blue, grey or pale skin, being hard to wake, or difficulty breathing.
For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact a GP.
A GP or NHS 111 should be contacted if a fever lasts 5 days or more.

body.heading: Can a fever be looked after at home?
body.body: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home. It recommends giving plenty of fluids and checking on the child regularly, including overnight.

body.heading: When does a fever need 999?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, or a first seizure caused by fever. The same list includes cold hands and feet, blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue, being drowsy and hard to wake, extreme agitation or confusion, and difficulty breathing. A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is described as non-blanching, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.

body.heading: When should NHS 111 or the GP be contacted?
body.body: For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact a GP. For babies aged 3 to 6 months, the NHS also advises calling NHS 111 or contacting a GP when the temperature is high. For older children, the NHS advises calling NHS 111 or contacting a GP when a fever has lasted 5 days or more. Signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes and no tears when crying, also call for advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What about rashes in babies?
body.body: Healthier Together pages say that most baby rashes are harmless and go away on their own, and that dry or peeling skin in the first week or two is normal. Tiny white or yellow spots on the nose or face (milia) usually clear within a few weeks without treatment. Healthier Together lists signs that need urgent help from a health professional: a rash that does not fade under the glass test, redness around the belly button, and a baby who is pale, very sleepy or breathing hard.

falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.name: Falls in older people and reducing the risk
falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.summary: Strength and balance exercises and simple changes at home can lower the risk of falls in older people, according to the NHS. NICE recommends offering falls prevention exercise programmes.
keyPoints: The NHS says the risk of falling can be lowered by exercises for strength and balance and by simple changes at home.
NICE guideline NG249 recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.
Clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping rooms and stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip are among the home-safety suggestions.
Regular sight tests are recommended, and in England the NHS provides free sight tests for people aged 60 or over.

body.heading: Why do falls happen?
body.body: Causes of falls include muscle weakness and balance changes with age, conditions that affect mobility or balance (such as arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's), low blood pressure, problems with eyesight or hearing, and dementia. Anyone can have a fall, but it is more likely in older people or those with mobility problems. Some medicines can affect balance and increase the chance of a fall. The NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist if medicines might be affecting balance. Postural hypotension is a drop in blood pressure on standing up from lying or sitting, which can cause dizziness and may lead to a fall.

body.heading: What exercise helps?
body.body: The NHS says regular exercises for strength and balance can improve strength and balance and reduce the risk of falls. The NHS notes there is evidence that regular tai chi can reduce the risk of falls. Programmes are described as best when tailored to the individual and overseen by a trained professional.

body.heading: What can be changed at home?
body.body: Suggestions include clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip. Regular sight tests are recommended, and free NHS sight tests are available to people aged 60 or over in England.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend?
body.body: NICE guideline NG249 covers falls assessment and prevention in older people and in people aged 50 and over at higher risk, and recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.

body.heading: What can a GP or falls team do?
body.body: A GP can check balance with simple tests, review medicines and refer to local falls services. Some areas have a falls team that offers a full assessment to older people who have fallen or are at high risk, and a GP surgery can say what is available locally.

body.heading: What does the NHS advise after a fall?
body.body: Advice after a fall includes calling for help, using a lifeline alarm if there is one, and keeping warm by covering up with a rug, blanket or towel. Advice for someone who is not hurt includes getting up slowly, and changing position regularly while waiting for help if they cannot get up. The NHS says to call 999 if someone has fallen and may have injured their head, back, neck or hip, cannot get up, is confused, drowsy or vomiting, or has severe bleeding; NHS 111 can help if they may be in pain, injured or unwell, and a GP can be seen after any fall.

hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.name: Hearing loss: causes, tests and what helps
hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.summary: Gradual hearing loss is common and a GP can arrange hearing tests. Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111, according to the NHS.
keyPoints: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or long-term exposure to loud noise.
A GP can look in the ears and may refer to an audiologist for a hearing test.
Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.
NHS hearing aids are free.

body.heading: What causes hearing loss?
body.body: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or to damage from loud noise over many years. Earwax, ear infections and a perforated eardrum are other common causes. Sensorineural hearing loss involves damage to the inner ear or the nerve pathway to the brain, while conductive loss means sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear, for example by earwax, fluid or infection.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP, and what happens?
body.body: Some pharmacies and opticians also offer a free hearing test. A GP can check for problems such as earwax or infection and may refer to an audiologist for further tests. If the GP finds no obvious cause, they should refer the person to an NHS audiologist for a full hearing assessment. In a common hearing test, the person wears headphones, hears sounds at different levels and presses a button each time they hear one. The test shows which pitches are affected and by how much.

body.heading: What if hearing is lost suddenly?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears. If neither is reachable, the nearest accident and emergency department is the route. Sudden hearing loss can be permanent, and treatment given early can reduce that risk. For sudden sensorineural loss the cause is often never found, and the usual treatment is steroids, which are most likely to help when given soon after the loss starts.

body.heading: What helps with permanent hearing loss and tinnitus?
body.body: For tinnitus, the first person to speak to is the GP, who can check the ears for treatable causes and may refer to a specialist. Treatable causes such as earwax or infection can often be dealt with by a GP, while permanent loss is usually managed with hearing aids. Hearing aids do not make hearing perfect, but they make sounds louder and clearer, and NHS hearing aids are free.

dementia-early-signs-and-assessment.name: Dementia: early signs and how it is assessed
dementia-early-signs-and-assessment.summary: Early signs of dementia include memory loss, trouble with familiar tasks and confusion about time or place. A GP starts the assessment, and a memory clinic may confirm the diagnosis.
keyPoints: NHS pages list memory loss, difficulty concentrating, trouble with familiar daily tasks, difficulty finding words, confusion about time and place, and mood changes as common early symptoms.
Memory can be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines, so the NHS suggests a GP visit for someone who is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly over 65.
A GP typically asks about symptoms, carries out an examination and arranges blood tests to look for other causes of memory problems.
A person may be referred to a memory clinic once reversible causes have been looked into and dementia is still suspected.

body.heading: What are the early signs?
body.body: Early symptoms are often mild and tend to progress very gradually. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, and vascular dementia is usually the second most common.

body.heading: Is forgetfulness always dementia?
body.body: The NHS says it is normal for memory to be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines. It suggests talking to a GP if someone is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly if they are over 65.

body.heading: What happens at the GP?
body.body: NICE says a history from someone who knows the person well can be supplemented with a structured tool such as the IQCODE. The NHS says a GP may arrange blood tests to rule out other causes of memory problems. NICE also recommends cognitive testing with a validated brief tool, and says a normal screening result alone should not rule dementia out. The NHS says there is no single test for dementia, and that diagnosis rests on a combination of assessments and tests. Memory and thinking tests usually start with a GP, and a specialist may later arrange brain scans such as a CT or MRI scan.

body.heading: When is a memory clinic involved?
body.body: NICE says dementia should be suspected after reversible causes such as delirium, depression, sensory impairment or the effects of some medicines have been looked into, and referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service applies if it is still suspected. The specialist assessment includes a neurological examination and cognitive testing, and a dementia subtype is diagnosed where possible. The first memory clinic appointment is usually long, and people are asked to bring someone who knows them well.

body.heading: What if it is unclear whether it is delirium or dementia?
body.body: NICE says that when it is unclear whether someone has delirium, dementia or both, the delirium is treated first. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion; NHS pages advise calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden confusion, because some causes can be life threatening and need prompt assessment.
